questions.stem: Which list gives the stages of the lifespan in order?
options: Infancy, childhood, early adulthood, adolescence, middle age, older age
Infancy, childhood, adolescence, early adulthood, middle age, older age
Childhood, infancy, adolescence, early adulthood, middle age, older age
Infancy, adolescence, childhood, early adulthood, middle age, older age
questions.explanation: The lifespan runs from infancy through childhood and adolescence to early adulthood, middle age and older age. The age boundaries between stages vary between sources, but the order does not.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a gross motor skill?
options: Threading small beads onto a piece of string
Picking up a sultana with finger and thumb
Writing your name neatly with a pencil
Running to catch a ball in the playground
questions.explanation: Gross motor skills use the large muscles of the arms, legs and trunk, as in running. Threading beads, a pincer grip and handwriting all use the small muscles of the hands and fingers, so they are fine motor skills.

questions.stem: Fine motor skills involve:
options: large movements using the muscles of the legs, arms and trunk
understanding and producing words and sentences
forming emotional bonds with caregivers and peers
small, precise movements, usually of the hands and fingers
questions.explanation: Fine motor skills are small, precise movements such as grasping, drawing and doing up buttons. Large movements of the legs and trunk are gross motor skills.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the usual order of language development in the first two years?
options: Cooing, first words, babbling, two-word utterances
Cooing, babbling, first words, two-word utterances
Babbling, cooing, two-word utterances, first words
First words, cooing, babbling, two-word utterances
questions.explanation: Infants coo with vowel sounds before they babble consonant-vowel strings, then produce first words and later combine two words. The ages vary between children, but the order is consistent.

questions.stem: A toddler cries and clings when her father leaves her with a babysitter. This is a change in which area of development?
options: Physical development (gross motor)
Physical development (fine motor)
Social and emotional development
Cognitive development (language)
questions.explanation: Distress at separation from a caregiver reflects the infant's emotional bond and social relationships, so it is social and emotional development. Nothing in the behaviour involves language or motor skills.

questions.stem: Which change is typical of older age?
options: Rapid growth in height and the production of many new neurons
The first appearance of abstract, hypothetical reasoning
The start of puberty and a sudden growth spurt
Slower reaction times and some decline in fine motor control
questions.explanation: Older age commonly brings slower reaction times and some loss of fine motor control. Growth spurts and puberty belong to adolescence, and abstract reasoning first appears in adolescence.

questions.stem: Learning to walk lets an infant explore more and meet more people, which gives her more chances to hear and use language. What does this show about the domains of development?
options: Each domain of development progresses completely independently
Social development stops once a child can walk unaided
Change in one domain can affect development in other domains
Physical development always happens after cognitive development
questions.explanation: The physical, cognitive, and social and emotional domains interact, so a gain in one, such as walking, opens opportunities in the others. The domains are studied separately, but they do not develop in isolation.

questions.stem: Neural plasticity is:
options: the loss of neurons that happens with ageing in older age
the brain's ability to change its structure and function with experience
the fixed sequence in which the brain's lobes grow before a baby is born
the fatty coating that speeds up messages along an axon
questions.explanation: Neural plasticity is the brain's capacity to reorganise its connections and functions as a result of experience. The fatty coating on axons is myelin, which is one product of development rather than plasticity itself.

questions.stem: Developmental plasticity refers to:
options: the brain compensating for function lost through injury
the decline in brain function that comes with ageing
the fixed size of the brain once childhood is over
changes in the brain as it develops, shaped by experience
questions.explanation: Developmental plasticity is the change in neural connections that occurs as the brain matures, following a set sequence but shaped by experience. Compensating for lost function after injury is adaptive plasticity.

questions.stem: After a stroke damages part of his left hemisphere, Peter slowly regains some speech as nearby areas take over the lost function. This is an example of:
options: developmental plasticity
synaptogenesis before birth
proliferation of neurons
adaptive plasticity
questions.explanation: Adaptive plasticity is the brain's ability to compensate for damage, for example by other areas taking over a lost function. Developmental plasticity is the change that happens as the brain matures.

questions.stem: Which list gives the stages of developmental plasticity in order?
options: Proliferation, synaptogenesis, migration, myelination, synaptic pruning
Synaptogenesis, proliferation, migration, synaptic pruning, myelination
Proliferation, migration, synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, myelination
Migration, proliferation, synaptogenesis, myelination, synaptic pruning
questions.explanation: Neurons are first produced (proliferation), move to their final positions (migration), form synapses (synaptogenesis), lose unused connections (synaptic pruning) and are coated with myelin (myelination). The stages overlap, but this is their order.

questions.stem: The rapid production of new neurons, mostly before birth, is called:
options: migration
synaptogenesis
myelination
proliferation
questions.explanation: Proliferation is the rapid production of new neurons, which happens mainly during prenatal development. Migration is the next stage, when the neurons move to where they will function.

questions.stem: In the migration stage of plasticity, neurons:
options: form new connections with other neurons
lose connections that are rarely used
become coated in a fatty insulating layer
move to their final positions in the brain
questions.explanation: During migration, newly formed neurons travel to the part of the brain where they will function. Forming new connections is synaptogenesis, which follows migration.

questions.stem: What happens during synaptogenesis?
options: Axons are coated in myelin to speed transmission
Neurons form new synapses with other neurons
Neurons move to their final positions in the brain
Unused synapses are eliminated to improve efficiency
questions.explanation: Synaptogenesis is the formation of new synapses, which is especially rapid in infancy. Eliminating unused synapses is synaptic pruning.

questions.stem: Synaptic pruning is often summed up as 'use it or lose it'. This means that:
options: new neurons are produced only in areas that are used frequently
rarely used synapses are removed and frequently used ones are kept
neurons that are rarely used move away to a different part of the brain
myelin is stripped from axons that carry only a few messages each day
questions.explanation: During synaptic pruning, connections that are seldom activated are removed and frequently used ones are kept and strengthened, making the brain more efficient. Pruning removes synapses, not myelin or whole areas.

questions.stem: Young infants can tell apart speech sounds from many languages, but by their first birthday they are less able to distinguish sounds not used in the language they hear. Which process best explains this?
options: Proliferation of new neurons after birth
Myelination of the auditory pathways
Synaptic pruning of rarely used connections
Migration of neurons to the temporal lobe
questions.explanation: Connections for speech sounds the infant rarely hears are seldom used and are pruned, while those for the home language are strengthened. Myelination speeds transmission but does not remove the ability to distinguish sounds.

questions.stem: Which statement about myelination is accurate?
options: It continues into early adulthood, and the frontal lobes are among the last areas finished
It is complete at birth in every area of the brain, which is why newborns can react to sounds
It is the process that removes rarely used synapses so the remaining connections work more efficiently
It happens before neurons have migrated to their final positions in the developing brain
questions.explanation: Myelination begins before birth but continues through adolescence and into early adulthood, with the frontal lobes, including the pre-frontal cortex, among the last areas to finish. Removing unused synapses is synaptic pruning.

questions.stem: During adolescence, which brain structure is generally more mature?
options: The amygdala
The pre-frontal cortex
The two are equally mature
Neither has begun developing
questions.explanation: The amygdala, involved in emotional responses, matures earlier than the pre-frontal cortex, which keeps developing into the mid-twenties. This imbalance helps explain some adolescent behaviour.

questions.stem: The amygdala is mainly involved in:
options: coordinating smooth movement and balance
relaying visual signals to the occipital lobe
processing emotions, especially fear and aggression
planning, organising and controlling impulsive behaviour
questions.explanation: The amygdala processes emotional responses, particularly fear and aggression. Planning and impulse control are functions of the pre-frontal cortex.

questions.stem: Why are adolescents often more likely than adults to take risks when they are with friends?
options: Their pre-frontal cortex has fully matured, but the amygdala is still undergoing proliferation
Synaptic pruning has removed most of the connections between the amygdala and the cortex
Their cerebellum is still developing, so they cannot judge the speed of hazards
Strong emotional responses are not yet matched by a fully mature pre-frontal cortex
questions.explanation: The amygdala, which drives emotional reactions, matures before the pre-frontal cortex, which is responsible for weighing consequences and controlling impulses. The pre-frontal cortex is one of the last areas to mature, not the first.

questions.stem: Sixteen-year-old Zac snaps angrily at a mildly critical comment from his coach, then later regrets it. Which explanation best fits current understanding of the adolescent brain?
options: Synaptic pruning has removed his ability to feel regret about past actions
His amygdala-driven reaction is not yet well regulated by his still-maturing pre-frontal cortex
His pre-frontal cortex is mature, but his amygdala has not yet completed migration
Myelination of the amygdala has made his emotional responses much slower to appear than an adult's
questions.explanation: In adolescence, the emotional amygdala is relatively mature, while the pre-frontal cortex, which moderates emotional responses, is still developing. Zac's later regret shows his reasoning is intact, but it did not regulate his reaction in the moment.

questions.stem: In Piaget's theory, a schema is:
options: an innate reflex present at birth, such as sucking or grasping
a test used to measure a child's level of thinking
a mental framework for organising knowledge about something
a stage of development reached at a particular age
questions.explanation: A schema is a mental framework or concept that organises knowledge about an object, event or action. Schemas are built and revised through assimilation and accommodation.

questions.stem: A two-year-old who knows the word 'doggy' points at a cow and says 'doggy'. Which process is shown?
options: Assimilation
Accommodation
Conservation
Seriation
questions.explanation: The child fits the new animal into an existing schema for four-legged animals, which is assimilation. Accommodation would happen when the child changes the schema or forms a new one for cows.

questions.stem: Her father explains that cows are bigger, say 'moo' and live on farms, and the child begins calling them 'cow'. This change in her schema is called:
options: centration
egocentrism
accommodation
assimilation
questions.explanation: Accommodation is changing an existing schema, or creating a new one, when new information does not fit. Assimilation fits new information into a schema without changing it.

questions.stem: According to Piaget, what motivates a child to accommodate new information?
options: Equilibrium, the comfort felt when new information fits easily into existing schemas
Egocentrism, the belief that others see the world from the child's own viewpoint
Conservation, the understanding that quantity stays the same when shape changes
Disequilibrium, the discomfort felt when new information does not fit existing schemas
questions.explanation: When new information does not fit existing schemas, the child experiences disequilibrium, which drives accommodation until equilibrium is restored. Equilibrium is the balanced state reached afterwards, not the motivator.

questions.stem: Object permanence is achieved in which of Piaget's stages?
options: Sensorimotor
Pre-operational
Concrete operational
Formal operational
questions.explanation: Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight, develops during the sensorimotor stage, from birth to about two years.

questions.stem: In an invisible displacement task, a toy is put in a small box, the box is moved under a cushion, the toy is left there, and the empty box is shown. A child with fully developed object permanence will:
options: search where the box was first placed
search under the cushion for the toy
search only inside the empty box
stop searching once the toy is hidden
questions.explanation: Searching under the cushion shows the child can mentally follow a movement they did not see, the mark of fully developed object permanence late in the sensorimotor stage. Searching only in the box means the child has not yet worked out the unseen move.

questions.stem: A four-year-old says the sun follows her car because it wants to come along. This is an example of:
options: seriation
object permanence
animism
conservation
questions.explanation: Animism, giving lifelike qualities such as wishes or feelings to non-living things, is typical of the pre-operational stage. Conservation and seriation develop later, in the concrete operational stage.

questions.stem: A three-year-old holds a banana to his ear and pretends to talk on the phone. Which feature of the pre-operational stage does this show?
options: Symbolic thinking
Egocentrism
Centration
Animism
questions.explanation: Using one object to stand for another in pretend play is symbolic thinking, a feature of the pre-operational stage. Egocentrism is difficulty seeing the world from another person's viewpoint.

questions.stem: In Piaget's three mountains task, a child picks the photo showing her own view of the model rather than the doll's view. This shows:
options: accommodation
egocentrism
centration
animism
questions.explanation: The three mountains task tests egocentrism, the inability to take another person's point of view, which Piaget saw as typical of the pre-operational stage. Choosing her own view shows she assumes the doll sees what she sees.

questions.stem: Juice is poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin one. Five-year-old Mei says the tall glass now holds more. Which explanation fits Piaget's theory?
options: She focuses only on the height and cannot mentally reverse the pouring
She lacks object permanence, so she forgets the first glass existed
She is egocentric, so she assumes the researcher sees a different glass
She is using abstract reasoning but has applied it to the wrong variable
questions.explanation: Mei fails the conservation task because of centration (focusing on one feature, the height) and a lack of reversibility. Object permanence was achieved in the sensorimotor stage, so it is not the problem here.

questions.stem: Arranging a set of sticks in order from shortest to longest is called:
options: centration
assimilation
seriation
conservation
questions.explanation: Seriation, putting items in order along a dimension such as length, is a skill of the concrete operational stage. Conservation is understanding that quantity stays the same when appearance changes.

questions.stem: A typical eight-year-old is in which of Piaget's stages?
options: Pre-operational
Formal operational
Sensorimotor
Concrete operational
questions.explanation: Piaget placed the concrete operational stage at about 7 to 11 years. Children in this stage can conserve and seriate, but they reason best about real objects rather than abstract ideas.

questions.stem: Fifteen-year-old Ruby debates what society would be like if nobody needed to sleep. Which stage does this kind of thinking show?
options: Sensorimotor
Formal operational
Concrete operational
Pre-operational
questions.explanation: Reasoning about hypothetical situations and abstract ideas is the hallmark of the formal operational stage, from about 11 or 12 years. Concrete operational thinkers reason logically, but mainly about real, present objects.

questions.stem: In Piaget's pendulum problem, which factor actually determines how quickly the pendulum swings?
options: The height it is released from
How hard it is pushed to start it
The length of the string
The weight on the end of the string
questions.explanation: Only the length of the string changes the time a pendulum takes to swing. Children who have not reached formal operations often wrongly decide that the weight or the push matters.

questions.stem: Which approach to the pendulum problem shows formal operational thinking?
options: Trying random combinations until the swing looks faster
Pushing harder each time, because force must matter most
Choosing the heaviest weight, because heavy things swing faster
Changing one factor at a time while keeping the others the same
questions.explanation: Formal operational thinkers test hypotheses systematically, varying one factor at a time while holding the others constant. Trial and error with random combinations is typical of concrete operational thinking.

questions.stem: Which is a recognised limitation of Piaget's theory?
options: He ignored thinking and focused only on emotional development
He underestimated what young children can do when tasks are made more familiar
He studied only adults and then generalised his findings to young children
He argued that development is gradual and continuous, with no distinct stages
questions.explanation: Later research found that young children often succeed at tasks such as perspective-taking when the tasks are made more familiar, suggesting Piaget underestimated them. Piaget studied children, and his theory is a stage theory of cognitive development.

questions.stem: A Year 3 teacher uses blocks and counters to teach subtraction. Which part of Piaget's theory supports this approach?
options: Sensorimotor children learn mainly by following abstract rules
Concrete operational children reason best about real, physical objects
Pre-operational children cannot use symbols of any kind
Formal operational thinkers learn mainly through handling physical objects
questions.explanation: Children in Year 3 are usually in the concrete operational stage, when they think logically but most easily about things they can see and handle. Formal operational thinkers can work with abstract ideas without concrete objects.
